title: Why Russia Sold Alaska for Under 2 Cents an Acre
summary: In 1867 Russia sold Alaska to the United States for $7.2 million in gold, under 2 cents an acre. Why Russia sold, how the treaty drew the line, whether 'Seward's Folly' was really what the country thought, and how big Alaska is next to the lower 48.
tags: why did the us buy alaska
sources: Permanent Russian settlers in Alaska never numbered more than four hundred; Russia offered to sell Alaska to the United States in 1859, believing the US would off-set the designs of Great Britain in the Pacific; the Civil War delayed the sale; defeat in the Crimean War further reduced Russian interest; Seward agreed to the purchase on March 30, 1867, for $7.2 million; the Senate approved the treaty April 9, 1867; Alaska was formally transferred October 18, 1867; skeptics had dubbed the purchase 'Seward's Folly'; gold found in the Yukon in 1896 made Alaska the gateway to the Klondike; Alaska's strategic importance was recognized in World War II; statehood January 3, 1959; the treaty ensured U.S. access to the Pacific northern rim (Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State, Milestones: Purchase of Alaska, 1867): https://history.state.gov/milestones/1866-1898/alaska-purchase

Treaty with Russia, March 30, 1867 (15 Stat. 539), Article I boundaries: in the east the 1825 Russian-British line, then the meridian of the 141st degree to the Frozen Ocean; in the west a line through Behring's Straits at 65 degrees 30 minutes north, midway between the islands of Krusenstern and Ratmanoff, due north into the Frozen Ocean and south-west through Behring's Sea; Article VI: seven million two hundred thousand dollars in gold; ratified May 28 and proclaimed June 20, 1867 (full text, Alaska State Library): https://library.alaska.gov/hist/fulltext/ASL-KF50.U58v15-p539.htm

Check for the Purchase of Alaska: a $7.2 million check dated August 1, 1868, payable to Russian Minister Edouard de Stoeckl; treaty signed March 30, 1867; the US acquired nearly 600,000 square miles for less than 2 cents an acre; critics called it 'Seward's Folly' (U.S. National Archives, Milestone Documents): https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/check-for-the-purchase-of-alaska

The fur trade in sea otter pelts slumped; the Hudson's Bay Company's economic ambition made the region vulnerable to British designs; after losing the Crimean War to Britain, France, and Turkey in 1856 the tsar was in no mood to see Alaska absorbed by a recent enemy; the tsar set $5 million as the lowest acceptable offer; in 1867 Seward agreed to purchase the territory for $7.2 million; Russia had to wait more than one year to be paid; expansionists saw Alaska as part of the American drive to the Pacific (Library of Congress, Meeting of Frontiers: The Alaska Purchase): https://www.loc.gov/collections/meeting-of-frontiers/articles-and-essays/alaska/the-alaska-purchase/

"Russia has sold us a sucked orange!" proclaimed the New York World; the Senate approved the treaty for ratification by a vote of 37 to 2 (U.S. Senate Historical Office, Sumner's Alaskan Project): https://www.senate.gov/about/powers-procedures/treaties/sumners-alaskan-project.htm

Of the fifteen 'national' periodicals consulted, only three expressed an editorial opinion adverse to the purchase (Leslie's Weekly, the New York Nation, Harper's Weekly); the author calls mistaken the view that virtually only Seward did not think it a folly (Richard E. Welch Jr., 'American Public Opinion and the Purchase of Russian America', American Slavic and East European Review, 1958, peer-reviewed): https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-slavic-and-east-european-review/article/american-public-opinion-and-the-purchase-of-russian-america/97D5334491B23ACC840DA1A846405311

Castle Hill, Sitka: place of the formal ceremony for the transfer of Russian America to the United States on October 18, 1867; the Russian flag was lowered and the United States flag raised (National Park Service, American Flag Raising Site): https://www.nps.gov/places/american-flag-raising-site.htm

Total area in square miles: United States (50 states and DC) 3,796,742; Alaska 665,384 (land 570,641); Hawaii 10,932; Texas 268,596; California 163,695; Montana 147,040 (US Census Bureau, State Area Measurements and Internal Point Coordinates, 2010): https://www.census.gov/geographies/reference-files/2010/geo/state-area.html.html
A normal section of land is one square mile, 640 acres (Bureau of Land Management, Land Legal Descriptions): https://or.blm.gov/or/landrecords/legaldescrip.php

Our arithmetic from the sources above: Alaska land area 570,641 sq mi x 640 acres = 365,210,240 acres; $7,200,000 / 365,210,240 acres = 1.97 cents an acre (about 2 cents; the National Archives says less than 2 cents). Lower 48 plus DC total area = 3,796,742 - 665,384 - 10,932 = 3,120,426 sq mi; Alaska's 665,384 is 21.3% of that (about a fifth). Texas + California + Montana = 579,331 sq mi, less than Alaska's 665,384.

When the world became aware of Klondike gold in 1897...; in 1899 thousands rushed to Nome; in 1903 a new strike on the Tanana River led to the founding of Fairbanks (National Park Service, Yukon-Charley Rivers: Klondike-Alaska Gold Rush): https://www.nps.gov/yuch/learn/historyculture/klondike-alaska-gold-rush.htm

From June 3 to 7, 1942, Japanese forces attacked Alaska's Aleutian Islands, invading the islands of Attu and Kiska (National Park Service, Battle of Attu): https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/battle-of-attu.htm

On January 3, 1959 President Eisenhower signed the proclamation admitting Alaska as the 49th state (Eisenhower Presidential Library, Alaska Statehood): https://www.eisenhowerlibrary.gov/research/online-documents/alaska-statehood

ARCO and Humble Oil and Refining Co. announced the Prudhoe Bay discovery well in March 1968; the pipeline spans 800.302 miles from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez; oil began flowing on June 20, 1977 (Ned Rozell, Alaska Science Forum, University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute, 24 Apr 1997): https://www.gi.alaska.edu/alaska-science-forum/twenty-years-pipe-changed-alaska

Map data: Natural Earth (public domain) https://www.naturalearthdata.com and US Census Bureau cartographic boundary files (public domain) https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/carto-boundary-file.html. The coral treaty lines are drawn approximately from the treaty's wording; the eastern line follows today's boundary.

scenes.narration: For about two cents an acre, the United States bought all of this from Russia.
That was {1867|eighteen sixty-seven}. So why would Russia sell? And why did America want it?
And that famous story, that Americans laughed at the deal and called it Seward's Folly? The record says something else.
By the end, you'll know why Russia sold, what America got, and how big Alaska really is next to the lower {48|forty-eight}.
Start on Russia's side. It held all this land with very few people. Permanent Russian settlers never numbered more than {400|four hundred}.

data.source: Office of the Historian, US State Dept.

scenes.narration: Its sea otter fur trade had slumped. And next door, the British Hudson's Bay Company had ambitions of its own.
Then, in {1856|eighteen fifty-six}, Russia lost the Crimean War to Britain, France and Turkey. The tsar didn't want Alaska absorbed by a recent enemy.
So in {1859|eighteen fifty-nine}, Russia offered Alaska to the United States, to offset Britain in the Pacific. Then the American Civil War got in the way.
If maps like this are your thing, subscribe. There's a new one every other day.
After the war, Secretary of State William Seward took up a new Russian offer. The treaty was signed in Washington on {March 30, 1867|March thirtieth, eighteen sixty-seven}.
The tsar's lowest price was {$5 million|five million dollars}. Seward agreed to {$7.2 million|seven point two million}, in gold. The money came over a year later.
Spread over Alaska's land, that's about two cents an acre. Our math, from Census figures.

data.source: US Census Bureau; BLM (640 acres = 1 sq mi)

scenes.narration: The treaty drew the line. In the east, the old Russian-British border, then up the {141st meridian|hundred and forty-first meridian} to the Arctic. In the west, a line through the Bering Strait.
On {October 18, 1867|October eighteenth, eighteen sixty-seven}, at Sitka, the Russian flag came down, and the American flag went up.
Now, that famous story. Critics did mock the deal. The New York World said Russia had sold us a sucked orange.
But historian Richard Welch checked {15|fifteen} national papers and magazines from the time. Only {3|three} came out against the purchase.

scenes.narration: And the Senate approved the treaty {37|thirty-seven} to {2|two}.
So the jokes were real, but they weren't the whole story. Most papers he checked, and almost the whole Senate, backed the deal.
Then Alaska paid off. In {1897|eighteen ninety-seven}, the world heard about Klondike gold, just across the border. In {1899|eighteen ninety-nine}, thousands rushed to Nome.

data.source: Office of the Historian; National Park Service

scenes.narration: In World War Two, Japan invaded Attu and Kiska, out in the Aleutians. Alaska's strategic value was finally clear.
On {January 3, 1959|January third, nineteen fifty-nine}, Alaska became the {49th|forty-ninth} state.
Then, in {1968|nineteen sixty-eight}, oil at Prudhoe Bay. And later, an {800|eight hundred}-mile pipeline south to Valdez.
So how big is it, really? Here it is beside the lower {48|forty-eight}.
By Census figures, Alaska's total area is about {21%|twenty-one percent} of the lower {48|forty-eight}'s. About a fifth. Our math.

data.title: One state, *one fifth*
data.source: US Census Bureau, 2010 areas; our arithmetic

scenes.narration: But it's still bigger than Texas, California and Montana put together.

data.source: US Census Bureau, total area; our sum

scenes.narration: So that's why the deal happened. Russia couldn't afford to hold Alaska, and America wanted its foothold on the North Pacific.
And for about two cents an acre, it got gold, a wartime frontier, and oil. So next time you see Alaska on a map, remember the price.
